problem: UX designers and design managers spend significant time in manual critique sessions reviewing screens for best practice compliance. Designers lack immediate feedback during the design process, and managers repeatedly flag the same issues across reviews. This tool automates the initial critique by analyzing a URL or screenshot and producing a structured heuristic evaluation report, so teams spend their session time on decisions rather than discovery.
audience: The primary users are UX designers who want to self-check their work before presenting it, and UX managers or design leads who review screens for quality and consistency. Both roles benefit from a faster, more structured first-pass review that surfaces issues before a live critique session.
data: The tool takes a URL or uploaded screenshot as input and produces a structured report containing identified heuristic violations, severity ratings (0-4 based on Nielsen's scale), and actionable recommendations per issue.
track: Design track. The tool is experienced primarily through its interface. The UI is the product: the designer interacts with it, reads the report, and acts on findings directly.
rationale: This project needs a great user interface more than backend computation. The core experience is submitting a URL or screenshot and reading a structured report, which is interface-first work. Lovable deploys fast and handles this interaction model well, with AI powering the analysis in the background.
title: Automated Heuristic UX Critique Report

problem: Friend groups often spend more time negotiating what to watch than actually getting excited about the movie. Existing tools recommend titles for individuals, but they don't make group taste compatibility visible, turning a simple movie night into a messy back-and-forth where preferences stay hidden, compromises feel random, and the final choice rarely feels like a shared win.
audience: Friend groups of 2–5 who watch together regularly.
data: Movie metadata (genres, tone, runtime, mood tags, ratings) pulled live from the TMDB API; user inputs are swipe-based ratings on 10 seeded movies per person and per-session blind auction bids; taste fingerprints and compatibility scores are computed from both inputs combined.
track: Design track the interface is the product. The value is in how the group experiences the negotiation together, visualized in real time as taste overlap and bid reveals.
platform: Cursor + TypeScript/React (web app) + Python (data layer); Figma MCP for design-to-code translation, Claude Code for computation logic.
rationale: The core work is computational; calculating taste fingerprints, running compatibility scoring across the group, and resolving auction logic which makes Cursor the right fit. Figma MCP allows interface designs to be translated directly into code without losing fidelity, and Claude Code accelerates the scoring logic and API integration in the terminal. Score Calculation: Swipe-based taste fingerprint Each person rates 10 TMDB-seeded movies via fast swipe yes / no / meh. The LLM maps each rated movie to its TMDB metadata vector (genre weights, tone, pacing, decade, runtime) and infers a personal taste profile, not just "likes action" but "likes slow-burn character-driven thrillers from the 90s." Group compatibility score = cosine similarity between each person's taste vector, averaged and visualized as a Venn overlap. The recommended movie sits in the intersection zone, not the loudest person's zone. Blind auction Each person gets 100 points per session, distributed secretly across nominated movies. No one sees anyone else's bids until reveal. The winner isn't simply highest total, the algorithm uses a max-min fairness model, weighting collective enthusiasm over individual passion. A movie that gets 30 points from everyone beats a movie that gets 80 from one person and nothing from the rest. This surfaces the movie nobody hates over the movie one person loves. Combined mode Taste fingerprint filters the full TMDB pool down to ~20 movies the group is genuinely compatible with. Blind auction then runs only on that shortlist, so you're bidding on 20 curated picks, not the entire internet.
title: Group Movie Taste Compatibility Finder

problem: Early career UX researchers and designers applying to multiple roles spend hours manually researching each company, reverse-engineering likely interview questions from job descriptions, and guessing which portfolio projects to highlight with no structured way to reuse or build on that work across applications.
audience: Entry level UX researchers and UX designers (0–3 years experience) actively job-hunting across multiple roles simultaneously. Mid and/or late career UX professionals could also benefit from this tool, but its large scale functionality meets the needs of those who are mass applying to internships and early career positions better.
data: The tool takes unstructured text inputs from the user (job descriptions, company notes, candidate background, etc.) and produces structured, role-specific prep content. Relevant interview questions, project recommendations, and talking points are generated via LLM and saved as JSON/markdown per session in the browser with the option of downloading to save.
track: Design track: The tool is experienced primarily through its interface, and the UI itself is the product. The LLM does the analytical heavy lifting, but the value the user experiences is a clean, organized prep workspace they can navigate, save, and return to.
platform: Bolt (Claude Code or Lovable as a close second)
rationale: This project needs complex conditional logic such as file uploads, multi-section form state, session persistence, tabbed output views, and dynamic LLM-driven rendering. These are all things that Bolt can handle well, along with the capability to make a UI forward product that deploys quickly.
title: UX Job Interview Prep Assistant

track: This project will be following the research track as it will help UX researchers and designers analyze and synthesize data from survey responses. The output is a structured report of the findings.

rationale: I've decided to use Cursor and Python because my project is primarily computation based. I will be processing, analyzing, and transforming CSV data so that my output can be insights to inform research.

audience: The primary users are HCD practitioners and product managers working on AI systems subject to the EU AI Act. Compliance officers and policy researchers who need to quickly assess documentation gaps across multiple systems also benefit.
data: The tool takes a user-supplied text input (product description, system documentation, or use case summary) and outputs a structured compliance gap analysis mapped to EU AI Act risk categories and requirements.
track: Research track. The tool analyzes input text and produces structured findings in the form of a compliance assessment report.
rationale: This project requires real computation, specifically parsing text, matching against regulatory criteria, and generating structured output, rather than primarily a visual interface. Cursor + Python is the right choice because the core work is text analysis and structured report generation, which maps directly to Python's strengths.
title: EU AI Act Compliance Gap Analyzer

problem: Student UX researchers often have to manually read open-ended survey responses and group them into themes before they can explain what users are struggling with.
audience: Student UX researchers use the tool after collecting survey feedback. Design teams benefit because they receive a frequency-ranked summary of user concerns instead of a long list of raw responses.
data: The tool uses a CSV of open-ended survey responses and produces a theme summary, frequency table, and short markdown report.
track: Research track.
platform: Cursor + Python, published as a Jupyter notebook on GitHub.
rationale: This project needs real computation because it processes, categorizes, and counts text responses. The interface is secondary, so Cursor + Python is a better fit than Lovable or Bolt.
title: Open-Ended Survey Theme Summarizer

problem: Women and wheelchair users are at great risk while going back home from campus at night. Finding reliable resources that provide access to community-sourced safety perceptions about specific campus routes, compels students to rely on outdated official crime data or word-of-mouth when deciding how to navigate the University District at night.
audience: UW students — primarily women and students with mobility needs — who navigate campus and surrounding neighborhoods on foot, especially during evening hours. Transit planners at Sound Transit and UW SafeCampus staff benefit downstream by gaining access to granular, community-reported safety perception data that official sources don't capture.
data: The tool I am intending to create draws from three sources: SPD open crime data (CSV, 2008–present), OpenStreetMap infrastructure data — lighting, ramps, curb cuts — both processed in Python, and Reddit posts scraped from r/Seattle, r/UWSeattle, and r/AskSeattle using the PRAW API. Reddit text is run through a Hugging Face sentiment classifier to extract safety perceptions and location mentions, surfacing which specific streets and areas women describe as unsafe in their own words. Together these form a baseline safety layer before a single user contributes a pin. The tool also produces ongoing community-contributed safety pins tagged with location, time of day, incident type, and optional photo, stored as GeoJSON.
track: Design track. The map, pin-dropping, accessibility layer toggle, and emergency resources are all experienced through the interface — the UI is the product.
platform: Cursor + Python for the data pipeline; Bolt for the frontend interface.
rationale: The project has two distinct layers — a computation layer processing SPD crime data, OSM infrastructure, and Reddit-derived safety signals into clean GeoJSON using Python, and an interface layer covering the map, pins, accessibility toggle, and emergency resources. Cursor handles the data work where Python is the right tool, and Bolt handles the UI where complex conditional interactions and fast deployment matter. How I am planning to build this The project is split into two parallel workstreams. In Cursor using Python, I will pull and clean the SPD crime dataset, query OpenStreetMap via the osmnx library to extract lighting infrastructure, curb cuts, and ramp locations around the University District, and scrape Reddit using PRAW for posts mentioning safety and Seattle neighborhoods. I will run a pre-trained Hugging Face classifier on the Reddit text to categorize safety sentiment and extract location mentions, then combine all three sources into a clean GeoJSON file that the frontend can consume as a pre-loaded baseline layer. In Bolt I will build the frontend — an interactive Leaflet.js map displaying the pre-loaded data, a pin-dropping interface where users can tag unsafe locations with time of day and incident type, a toggleable accessibility layer showing wheelchair-accessible routes and infrastructure, and a one-tap emergency resources tab with UW SafeCampus, UWPD, and crisis line contacts. Before building I will run a short survey of 15–20 UW students to validate assumptions and inform design decisions, particularly around the companion walking feature. Planned features (not finalised yet- will finalize these based on user research) Community safety map — the core of the app. Pre-loaded with SPD crime data and Reddit-derived safety signals as a baseline. Users drop pins on locations that feel unsafe, attach a photo, select time of day and incident type. Pins are visible to all users and accumulate over time. Accessibility layer — a toggleable overlay showing wheelchair-accessible routes, curb cuts, ramp locations, and surface quality sourced from OpenStreetMap. No existing safety tool combines mobility accessibility with safety perception in one place — this is the design contribution. Emergency resources — one-tap access to UW SafeCampus, UWPD, and campus crisis lines. Always visible, never buried in a menu. Walking companion board — scoped as future work, informed by survey findings. Users post where they are leaving from, where they are going, and what time. Others can join. Trust is built through UW email verification, completed walk badges, and anonymous post-walk safety confirmations. Designed deliberately after research rather than before it. Safe route suggester — also future work. Suggests a well-lit, lower-risk route weighted by community pins and OSM lighting data, even if slightly longer than the fastest path. Requires graph computation beyond the current scope.
title: UW Campus Safety Perception Map

problem: UX researchers setting up a new study manually write and assemble consent forms, reminder emails, and session scripts each time, so study setup takes longer than it should and details get missed.
audience: UX researchers and designers
data: The researcher inputs study name, date, participant name, method type, and their own session script and tasks; selects a consent form type from predefined options; the tool automatically generates a Zoom link via Zoom API and outputs a complete packet containing a consent form ready to send to participant, a participant confirmation email with the Zoom link, a 24-hour reminder email sent automatically before the session, and a session script with tasks both as provided by researcher.
track: Research track — the tool helps researchers set up and execute a study by generating the operational documents needed to run it. The outputs are structured research artifacts
rationale: The tool requires real computation i.e. a Zoom API call to generate the session link and a backend scheduler to trigger the reminder email 24 hours before the session. Bolt handles both the interface and the backend logic.
title: UX Study Document Auto-Generator

problem: Bystanders responding to cardiac arrest emergencies often struggle to quickly locate nearby automated external defibrillators (AEDs) and access critical response information under stress, making it harder to coordinate actions efficiently during emergency situations.
audience: Bystanders and emergency responders use the system during emergency situations to quickly access guidance and locate nearby AEDs. Patients and emergency responders benefit from faster and more informed emergency actions.
data: The tool uses public AED location datasets (such as OpenStreetMap AED data) and simulated emergency interaction data to generate guidance and rescue summaries.
track: Design Track
rationale: Bolt is appropriate because the project depends on interactive workflows, location-based information, and conditional user actions rather than only data processing. The system requires multiple connected interfaces, such as emergency guidance, AED mapping, and rescue flow interactions, where the user experience is central to helping people act quickly under stressful situations.
title: Emergency AED Locator and Guide

problem: A tool that helps UX researchers and service designers analyze behavioral and emotional patterns in shared mobility systems by processing large-scale e-scooter trip data, so teams do not have to rely only on interviews or manual observation to understand how people actually use urban transportation services in real contexts.
audience: The primary users are UX researchers, service designers, and urban mobility product teams working on transportation platforms such as Lime or Bird. City planners and operations teams could also benefit from understanding when, where, and how users experience friction in scooter usage, parking behavior, and transportation access.
data: The tool uses the Seattle Shared Scooter Trips dataset from the City of Seattle Open Data portal, which contains trip-level data including start time, end time, trip duration, scooter provider, and geographic information in CSV format. Python and pandas clean, filter, and analyze usage patterns, peak demand periods, trip behaviors, and operational trends, generating visual summaries and insight reports.
track: Research track
rationale: This project is centered on computational analysis of large-scale behavioral datasets rather than interface interaction design. Cursor and Python are the best fit because the main challenge is processing structured trip data, identifying patterns across time and geography, and translating quantitative findings into research insights that could inform transportation and service design decisions.
title: Urban Scooter Trip Pattern Analyzer

problem: The problem that I want to help tackle is that when public health evaluators synthesize interview notes and field observations by hand, low-literacy participant voices often get quietly paraphrased into cleaner, more academic language. This tool flags those moments so evaluators can catch and fix them before findings are finalized.
audience: The primary audience is public health evaluators, people who are responsible for turning raw qualitative data into structured findings for funders, policy makers, or health departments. The people who benefit from it are low-literacy non-English speakers whose voices need to be present in the findings.
data: The tool takes qualitative research notes from program evaluators as input (txt, docx, and pdf files).
track: Research track- the notes go in, the tool analyzes them, and flagged passages come out for the evaluator to review. The output is the point, not the interface.
rationale: The reason why lovable will be a good platform for this problem is that the core interaction of the tool will be uploading notes, reviewing highlighted flags, accepting or dismissing warnings, and exporting findings. It is interface-driven rather than computation-heavy
title: Low-Literacy Voice Preservation Checker

problem: This tool would help HCD students and interface designers choose accessible color pairings for UI components such as text, buttons, cards etc so they don't have to manually check their contrast ratios or assume whether or not their visual design choices are accessible/readable.
audience: The primary users for this are HCD students, UI designers and product designers who are creating things like interface mockups, visual design systems or mid/high fidelity prototypes. The people that would benefit are those using the interface, especially users that have visual impairments (like low vision, color vision differences), as well as those using the interface with certain situational visibility constraints (like when it's nighttime or there's screen glare etc), as the design would be easier to read and use.
data: The tool uses color values entered by the designer as HEX codes for UI components like text, buttons, backgrounds, or interface states, and produces contrast ratios, pass or fail guidance, accessible color alternatives, and visual previews of the pairings in common UI components.
track: This fits the Design track, since this tool would be experienced primarily through its interface and visual previews. The purpose is more to help designers make better/more accessible visual UI decisions when they are actively working with color, instead of only generating a summary of insights.
rationale: I think Bolt will be the best fit for building this tool because the project would require real computation as well as an interactive interface. The tool would have to do things like calculate contrast ratios, apply certain pass/fail rules, generate alternative color pairings (if necessary), and then show live previews in realistic interface components and so I think Bolt would be best for this as this requires complex interactions and computation in response to user input.
title: Accessible UI Color Pairing Tool

problem: When UX researchers are in the process of creating a readout deck, they already know the theme they want to show (e.g, “this person only wanted listings with a pool”), but their notes are mostly paraphrased, so they end up Ctrl+F-ing the transcript, guessing keywords, and skipping through long recordings trying to figure out which participant actually said it and what the exact quote was.
audience: UX researchers would use this on their own when they’re pulling evidence for a slide deck, even if they’re part of a bigger team. Researchers have credibilty when the presenter can name the participant and back up the theme with a real quote and timestamp, not just “someone mentioned pools.”
data: Researchers upload (or link out from) timestamped transcripts and optional video per participant and type the vague gist of what they’re looking for and maybe a keyword or which participant they think it was, so the tool spits back verbatim participant lines with timestamps and who said it (no AI summary, just the raw quotes to check).
track: Research
rationale: This feels more computally-heavy, since the code needs to actually find the right lines across long transcripts and multiple people when a user only remembers the gist. Cursor + Python is good for that kind of search/ranking work, whereas in my experience Lovable and Bolt focus less on complex functionality and moreso UI aesthetics.
title: Qualitative Transcript Quote Finder

problem: Font selection is a slow, often overwhelming part of the design process. Designers spend significant time browsing typefaces without a clear way to filter by design intent or know which fonts will work together. This tool addresses that by giving users a structured, guided way to find and pair fonts — and walk away with a usable type system.
audience: Anyone working on a design project — professional designers, students, or people building personal brands. Users may not have a strong design background, so the tool needs to guide rather than overwhelm. The interaction should feel approachable enough to complete in roughly 30 minutes.
data: The tool pulls font data from a font API (Google Fonts is the likely candidate). Each font is organized by attributes including typeface category, mood, use case, and weight options. Users can filter by these attributes to narrow their options. Once a primary font is selected, the tool suggests compatible pairings for a second font.
track: Design track: The interface and design elements is the core of this project. The value is in the guided selection flow and the live rendered preview, not in any computation happening behind the scenes.
platform: Given the multi-step user flow (filter → select → pair → preview → export) and the dynamic font loading, Bolt is the stronger fit. However, I also have access to Claude Code, and I was wondering if I could use that in my Cursor terminal.
rationale: For Bolt, I thought it would be a good fit to build the final product, considering that this project is front-end and design-based. That is also why I thought Claude Code could also be a good fit because it could easily be integrated into my Cursor workflow and also build a front-end design tool.
title: Guided Font Selection and Pairing Tool

problem: This idea stems from a human-centered design problem that I often face when I see portfolios or nicely developed websites in the wild, and it's that I don't have an organized way to save everything save for my gigantic "Portfolio" bookmark folder. Additionally, I also have to save whole websites for small interactions and often forget why later on, because I have no way to annotate my saved websites. When I'm looking for inspiration for my portfolio or a project, I have to spend extra time to click through my bookmarks and try to remember why I saved a specific website.
audience: This is mostly aimed at other product designers, or even design engineer type roles. Anyone that works in web design, although I could also see many students (such as myself) using this too.
data: The data required for this project to work mostly involves screenshots and/or screen recordings of different websites, added by the users themselves. Other data includes user-entered data about the screenshots/screen recordings, such as website URL, descriptions, annotations, or potential development tools to note down.
track: This project falls under the Design track. My idea is for this project to take the form of a macOS based extension/app pinned above every window, so that users can access it quickly but it still remains out of the way of their daily work.
platform: Probably Bolt because my project has a significant UI component. However, it also requires some backend establishment (especially as I figure out how to actually make a macOS widget/app/extension), so maybe Cursor will be needed for those aspects too. Claude for planning.
rationale: Probably Bolt because my project has a significant UI component. However, it also requires some backend establishment (especially as I figure out how to actually make a macOS widget/app/extension), so maybe Cursor will be needed for those aspects too. Claude for planning.
title: Annotated Design Inspiration Collector

problem: UX researchers analyzing interview transcripts or open-ended survey responses often spend hours manually identifying important quotes and grouping responses into themes while trying to maintain clear evidence for their findings.
audience: UX researchers and HCI students use the tool during early-stage qualitative analysis to organize qualitative data more efficiently. The tool helps research teams identify recurring themes and supporting participant quotes before affinity mapping sessions, presentations, or synthesis discussions.
data: The tool takes qualitative text data such as interview transcripts, usability session notes, or open-ended survey responses and produces grouped themes with representative supporting quotes.
track: Research track
rationale: The project focuses on helping researchers analyze and synthesize qualitative data through AI-assisted theme grouping and quote extraction. Cursor supports the computational processing of qualitative text data, while Lovable enables an interactive interface where researchers can review, refine, and reorganize AI-generated thematic groupings and supporting evidence.
title: AI-Assisted Qualitative Theme Grouper

problem: UX researchers conducting qualitative interviews waste time manually writing follow-up questions mid-session and spend hours after each interview hand-coding notes into themes; this tool generates deeper questions before the interview and produces a structured summary from an uploaded audio recording so researchers can focus on listening instead of logistics.
audience: The primary users are UX researchers and design students who conduct qualitative user interviews as part of their research process. They benefit by getting AI-generated follow-up questions before the session and a structured summary of themes, friction points, and key quotes immediately after — without manual synthesis.
data: The tool takes a researcher-entered topic and starter questions as text input, and an uploaded audio file (mp3/m4a) recorded during the interview; it produces an AI-generated transcript via Whisper and a structured summary via Claude.
track: Design track — the tool is experienced primarily through its interface, with three distinct views (Setup, Interview, Results) that guide the researcher through a session end-to-end.
platform: Cursor + React — the tool requires real computation including audio file upload, transcription via OpenAI Whisper, and AI summarization via Anthropic Claude, which requires a proper development environment rather than a no-code builder.
rationale: This project has two external API integrations (Whisper for transcription, Claude for question generation and summarization) and a file upload flow — that complexity is past what Bolt or Lovable handle cleanly. Cursor gives full control over the API calls, file handling, and debugging needed to make the core functionality work reliably.
title: AI Interview Prep and Synthesis Tool

problem: A tool that pulls SurveyMonkey feedback data broken down by individual coaching class, so the coaching operations manager doesn't have to manually work around an aggregate-only dashboard that can't filter or segment by class.
audience: The primary user is the coaching operations manager responsible for overseeing classes, a non-technical stakeholder who needs fast, self-serve access to class-level feedback. Coaches may also use it occasionally to review feedback on their own sessions and improve their delivery.
data: The tool uses participant survey responses exported from SurveyMonkey (pulled automatically via the SurveyMonkey API or uploaded as a CSV) and produces filtered, class-level dashboard views of that feedback.
track: Design track, the interface is the product. The value is in giving non-technical users a clean, interactive dashboard they can navigate without any manual data wrangling.
rationale: There is a potential PHI/PII risk: although unlikely, open-text survey feedback could contain protected health or personally identifiable information so I don't think I can use a tool like Bolt or Loveable. This can run locally, would keep all data on-device and never send it to a third-party service. This could be built with an interactive dashboard component to keep it simple enough for non-technical users. A hosted/shared option could also be offered as an optional upgrade once compliance is confirmed.
title: Class-Level Coaching Feedback Dashboard

problem: Beginner developers who want to contribute to open source struggle to identify repositories and contribution opportunities that match their skills, confidence, and learning goals, and currently must rely on GitHub search, static filters, or generic AI prompts that provide limited guidance about project fit or onboarding difficulty.
audience: The primary users are beginner developers and early-career programmers exploring open source contribution. They benefit from guidance in identifying approachable repositories and contribution opportunities that align with their technical background and confidence level.
data: The prototype uses user interview responses captured through the website application and public GitHub repository data (fetched through github API), including repository descriptions, README files, issue metadata, and labels - and produces structured preference profiles and AI-generated repository recommendations with explanations.
track: Design track
rationale: This project is experienced primarily through a web interactive interface where adaptive preference elicitation (asking beginner developers for their preferences) and recommendation explanations shape the user experience. Cursor is appropriate because the prototype requires conversational flows, conditional questioning, and real-time recommendation logic rather than heavy computational analysis alone. Note: I have already fetched repository data (data from 100 repositories) from github API as I continue to work on the project.
title: Open Source Contribution Recommender

problem: ResearchBridge aims to bridge the gap between UX professionals with their stakeholders and business partners (leadership, product, engineering, etc.) by generating insights and actionable tickets tailored to the audience and environment.
audience: The primary user is a UX researcher or designer who has completed a study and needs to communicate findings across disciplines. The primary beneficiaries are product managers and engineers, who receive clearer, actionable, audience-appropriate outputs without needing to read a full research report.
data: The tool takes unstructured research artifacts as input — PDFs, DOCX files, Notion exports, or plain text transcripts — and produces structured text outputs in the form of audience-specific insight briefs and formatted user stories with embedded evidence quotes and acceptance criteria.
track: Both Research & Design track. The interface is the product — researchers interact with ResearchBridge through a UI that handles file upload, audience selection, and output review. The AI processing happens in the background, but the value is experienced through reading, editing, and exporting the generated outputs.
platform: Bolt and/or Cursor with consideration complexity of functionality and whether my credit limit creates friction (Cursor I have a student account with pro lvl credits so even if Bolt is better for scaffolding UI I may get further in Cursor)
rationale: ResearchBridge needs more than a pretty interface — it requires real computation in response to user input: parsing uploaded documents, calling the Anthropic API with structured prompts (built in AI agent for this tool), and dynamically generating different outputs based on which audiences are selected. Lovable would handle the UI well but struggles with file handling and conditional API logic; Bolt supports the reactive, input-driven computation this workflow depends on while still producing a deployable interface quickly.
title: Audience-Specific Research Brief Generator

problem: Legal-tech researchers currently read Reddit and the open web by hand to find recurring complaints and adoption signals about legal AI; this tool collects that public discourse and produces Charmaz-style thematic insights so they do not spend days manually coding before a market or UX readout.
audience: I use it as a legal-tech and HCD researcher tracking how lawyers and practitioners talk about legal AI and tools. UX researchers and product managers at legal-tech companies (e.g. Harvey, Legora) benefit from frequency-ranked themes and quoted evidence for positioning, roadmap, and competitive insight.
data: It ingests public text from Reddit (API) plus other lawful open sources (e.g. legal-tech blogs, public LinkedIn posts, OSS READMEs with cited claims), stores raw and processed rows as CSV, and outputs a coded corpus with Charmaz-informed categories, theme statements, memos, and illustrative excerpts.
track: Research track: collect, analyze, and synthesize; primary outputs are a Jupyter notebook, CSV datasets, and thematic insights (visualization optional later).
rationale: This project needs real computation—fetching public posts, cleaning text, coding excerpts, and aggregating themes—not a polished consumer UI as the main deliverable. Cursor + Python supports a notebook + CSV + grounded-theory pipeline, with an optional lightweight local UI later for exploration only. Questions for Brock/ Alyse: 1. Does this project cover the assignment expectations? 2. I am thinking of using something creative like teachable machines, or something to train lawyer's arguments or witness prep depositions in real time, but I don't know if that would satisfy the assignment criteria. How does that addition sound?
title: Legal AI Public Discourse Analyzer

problem: Solo qualitative researchers who use LLMs like Claude or ChatGPT during coding and thematic analysis make dozens of small interpretive decisions per session (accepting an AI-suggested code, modifying a theme, rejecting a paraphrase) but currently have no structured way to capture the reasoning behind those decisions, leaving methods sections vague and audit trails reconstructed from memory weeks later.
audience: The primary user is a graduate student or early-career qualitative researcher in HCI, CSCW, or adjacent fields who uses an LLM as a thinking partner mid-analysis on a small-sample interview study. The tool also benefits methods instructors and IRB reviewers who need a defensible way to evaluate AI-assisted qualitative work without prescribing a single workflow.
data: Input is a researcher-AI chat transcript exported from Claude or ChatGPT (JSON or pasted text); output is a structured decision matrix in CSV and Markdown documenting each AI interaction, what the researcher accepted, modified, or rejected, the stated reasoning, the analytic phase, and an extractor-confidence flag.
track: Research track.
rationale: The core work is computation: parsing chat transcripts, running structured LLM prompts to extract decision points, and aggregating them into an inspectable matrix and exportable artifacts, not interface design. Publishing as a GitHub notebook aligns with academic norms for methodological tools and lets reviewers inspect the schema, the prompt, and the validation harness directly, which is the intellectual contribution.
title: AI-Assisted Qualitative Decision Auditor

problem: UX students, junior designers, and developers on small product teams can identify interface violations through heuristic or accessibility evaluation, but must manually reason through design principles and write specific recommendations from scratch, this tool will take screenshots and a brief description of the UI and give actionable steps and recommendations for UX professionals and product teams to work with.
audience: The primary users are UX/HCD students conducting expert evaluations for coursework and junior designers completing audits for clients or internal teams. A secondary audience is developers and product managers on small teams who receive evaluation findings but lack the design background to interpret or act on them.
data: The tool takes a user-uploaded screenshot of any digital interface as input and produces a structured evaluation report containing heuristic violations, WCAG accessibility issues, severity ratings, effort estimates, and specific plain-language recommendations for each finding.
track: Design track. The tool is experienced entirely through its interface, the user uploads a screenshot, reads a structured report, and acts on recommendations. The UI is the product.
platform: Cursor + Claude + Vercel I chose these tools to build the project on since I will not run out of tokens as I have the cursor education plan and Claude Pro. Vercel will allow me to deploy free on the base tier.
rationale: The core intelligence lives in the Claude API call and the system prompt that structures the JSON output, that is computation responding to user input, not a passive display layer. Cursor is the right choice because the meaningful work is wiring a vision model to a structured output and rendering it correctly, not designing a marketing-style interface. Although I have some Claude skills that could help me create a cleaner UI.
title: Screenshot-Based UI Heuristic Evaluator

problem: Over 5 million neurodivergent students in India, including children with dyslexia, ADHD, and autism, currently learn through mainstream EdTech platforms like Byju's, Duolingo, and government e-learning apps that offer no cognitive adaptation, forcing them to navigate visually overloaded, comparison driven interfaces that trigger sensory overwhelm and shutdown, or go without digital learning support entirely.
audience: Primary users are neurodivergent learners aged roughly 10 to 16 in Indian classrooms who need control over reading pace, font (including OpenDyslexic), color contrast, and motion in order to engage with content. Secondary beneficiaries are educators like the teacher in my prior research who said "I have 40 students and no tools," who would use the platform to support differentiated instruction without building scaffolds from scratch.
data: The app uses a small curated library of reading passages paired with learner controlled UI state (font, pace, contrast, audio toggle, motion level) set during onboarding, plus self paced progress milestones stored locally to celebrate individual gains without comparison.
track: Design track. The interface is the intervention; accessibility lives in typography, motion control, and audio synchronized reading rather than in backend computation.
rationale: This is a design track project where the entire research insight lives in the interface, including accessible typography, customization first onboarding, motion control, and audio synchronized reading, so the deciding question (computation or interface) lands clearly on interface. Lovable is the right tool because it lets me deploy a real, accessible web app fast without spending the project's limited time on framework setup or hosting, which keeps the focus on the UX decisions my research demands.
title: Adaptive Reading App for Neurodivergent Learners

problem: — HCD designers lose the reasoning behind their in-progress decisions because reflection only happens after the fact, forcing them to reconstruct rationale from memory when writing handoffs, case studies, or portfolio documentation.
audience: — Mid-level HCD and UX designers working inside Figma on active projects who want to document their process but deprioritize it under deadline pressure. Design leads who need to hand off decision rationale to collaborators also benefit.
data: — The designer selects a Figma frame or pastes text as a work anchor, responds to a card-drawn prompt, and the tool produces a structured reflection document written in their own words, stored locally via figma.clientStorage. This helps design practitioners grow their practice.
track: — Design track: the plugin interface is the ritual — the UI is the product.
rationale: — This project requires a Figma plugin, which Lovable and Bolt cannot scaffold — it needs direct access to the Figma Plugin API and its native storage layer. The document generation logic and card system also involve real computation that benefits from Cursor's code-first environment over a drag-and-drop builder.
title: In-Progress Design Decision Reflector

problem:
People who want to creatively engage with the night sky have no tool that lets them invent personal constellations from imagination and see them mapped onto real stars — so this tool lets anyone draw a shape using 
**straight-line segments**
 on a sketch pad, have 
**each vertex automatically snapped**
 to the nearest real catalog star, and receive an 
**AI-generated name**
 for the constellation they just created.
audience:
The primary users are the 
**general public**
, 
**astronomy hobbyists**
, and 
**artists**
 — people who find the night sky beautiful and want a low-friction, playful, visually rich way to interact with real stellar data without needing any astronomical background. 
**Educators and science communicators**
 are a welcome secondary audience but not the primary framing — the tool is built for 
**curiosity and creative expression**
 first.
data:
The tool uses the 
**HYG v4.2**
 star catalog pre-filtered to 
**~9,000 naked-eye-visible stars**
 (
`mag < 6.5`
), prepared by a Python script (
`prepare_stars.py`
) and hosted as 
**
`stars_visible.csv`
**
 with fields: 
`id`
, 
`ra`
, 
`dec`
, 
`mag`
, 
`ci`
, 
`spect`
, 
`lum`
, 
`proper`
, 
`dist`
, 
`x`
, 
`y`
, 
`z`
 — loaded 
**client-side**
 in the browser; user-generated constellation names are 
**optionally**
 checked for global uniqueness against a 
**Supabase 
`used_names`
**
 table, but 
**full constellation records are not persisted**
.
track:
**Design track**
 — the product is experienced entirely through its interface: the immersive galaxy star map, the straight-line sketch pad, the snap-to-star result projected onto real stars, the 
**2D/3D toggle**
, and the 
**PNG export**
. The computation (vertex normalisation, nearest-neighbour snap, Claude API naming call) is invisible infrastructure in service of the creative experience.
platform:
**Lovable**
 — with the 
**Claude API**
 called via Lovable's built-in edge function support for AI naming, and 
**optional Supabase**
 for a lightweight used-names registry only.
rationale:
The product's value is almost entirely in how it looks and feels — an immersive 
**galaxy aesthetic**
 in 
**Roboto Mono**
, a smooth draw-to-constellation experience, and a beautiful 
**2D/3D result**
 — which makes Lovable the right choice because the interface is the product and Lovable deploys a polished React frontend faster than any alternative. The 
**nearest-neighbour snap**
 across ~9,000 stars runs fast enough 
**client-side in JavaScript**
 without any compute backend, so there is no technical argument for Bolt at this data scale.
title: Personal Constellation Creator

problem: I want to make a tool for UX researchers who are doing usability testing. The tool will take raw usability session notes, transcripts and usability session recordings and conduct some thematic analysis and qualitative analysis on them to produce a structured summary of recurring themes, so that UX researchers don't have to spend a long time manually working through each transcript and notes.
audience: It is intended for UX researchers. They will benefit from it by saving the time that they would spend on working through notes and transcripts.
data: It produces a spreadsheet of themes, supporting quotes, source transcript or recording, and analysis.
track: - Research track: the tool helps you collect, analyze, or synthesize data — outputs are insights, summaries, or structured findings
platform: - Cursor + Python: the right choice when the work is primarily computation — processing, analyzing, transforming data
rationale: I want to use Cursor + python because the work is primarily computation. I need to process the notes, transcripts and voice recordings, and then get it to analyze them, group them into themes, and then produce some structured notes.
title: Usability Session Theme Synthesizer

problem: A tool that takes raw research notes or findings and automatically rewrites them as stakeholder-specific summaries, so researchers don't have to manually reframe the same insight four different ways before a cross-functional readout.
audience: Early-career UX researchers and design students who are new to working cross-functionally. They have the research skills but haven't yet developed fluency in translating findings for engineers, PMs, or business stakeholders.
data: The user inputs free-form text such as research notes, interview summaries, or written findings, and the tool produces multiple rewritten versions of that input, each tailored to a specific stakeholder role.
track: Research track- the tool takes user-provided research data and produces structured, audience-specific insight summaries as output.
rationale: This project requires real AI computation in response to user input, as it will transform text into multiple stakeholder-specific outputs. Bolt supports the combination of conditional logic, AI calls, and a designed interactive experience.
title: Stakeholder-Tailored Research Summary Tool

problem: A tool that takes a single SVG design template and produces multiple customised variants with different text, colours, images, and fonts, so designers and marketers do not have to manually duplicate and edit files one by one in Figma or Illustrator.
audience: The primary users are graphic designers, marketers, and creative professionals who need to produce design assets at scale, but the tool is built to be simple enough for anyone to use. This includes a person making wedding invitations, a small business owner creating promotional cards, or a professional in a non-creative field who wants to explore design variants in different styles or languages without needing to know any design software.
data: The tool takes a user-uploaded SVG file and an optional CSV of variable data as input, then produces rendered output files in SVG, PDF, or PNG format, with the option to push all variants directly into a Figma file so users can open, edit, or refine each one individually. All variant definitions are stored as JSON during the session.
track: Design track. The interface is the product. The drafting board, the AI chat panel, the layer detection UI, and the variant preview grid are what make this tool useful and accessible to a wide range of people.
rationale: The tool relies on real computation to parse SVG files, map data to layers, call the Gemini API for AI-driven generation, and batch render output files at scale. The interface is important for making that pipeline feel simple and intuitive, but the processing and automation happening underneath is what drives the core value.
title: Batch SVG Design Variant Generator

problem: A tool that scans interview and survey protocols during the first draft and flags leading language, hidden assumptions, and inconsistent phrasing across moderators, so UX and human-subjects researchers catch wording that produces unreliable, biased data.
audience: UX researchers, survey builders, and other human-subjects researchers use the tool while drafting protocols, and peer reviewers use it during informal review. Participants get fairer questions, stakeholders receive more trustworthy findings, and moderators stay aligned on phrasing — supporting research integrity without a formal team workflow.
data: The tool takes interview/survey protocol text via paste or .docx upload and outputs per-question bias flags, template-based rewrite suggestions, and question-level bias scores, using a rule-based detection layer built from survey methodology and UX research language guidelines.
track: Research Track: The tool analyzes protocol text and produces structured findings — per-question bias flags, scores, and rewrite suggestions — not a polished writing experience as the main product. A simple UI (e.g. Streamlit) is just how researchers submit text and read results.
rationale: This project needs real computation — parsing questions, matching bias patterns, scoring, and comparing moderator versions — more than it needs a polished interface. Cursor + Python fits that workflow: you can build and iterate on the rule-based logic quickly and ship a working demo in two weeks without front-end overhead.
title: Research Protocol Bias Detector

problem: UX researchers who record moderated usability sessions currently have to manually review video footage, transcribe notes, and code findings before a readout, which takes three or more hours per session and misses behavioral signals like facial confusion and vocal stress that only exist in the recording, not the transcript.
audience: UX researchers and designers who conduct moderated usability testing and record sessions with screen and camera capture. Researchers working under tight deadlines benefit most because they are the ones most likely to skip behavioral evidence when time pressure forces them to rely on text-only AI synthesis.
data: The tool takes video, audio, text files or any combination of the three from usability sessions containing simultaneous screen recording, camera feed, and participant audio. It uses multiple APIs to collect and process this data: Whisper for audio transcription, wav2vec2 for vocal emotion analysis, GPT-4o vision for facial expression and screen state analysis, and Mistral via the HuggingFace Inference API for language analysis and report generation. ChromaDB stores and clusters findings across sessions. The tool produces structured findings organised by friction cluster, severity, and heuristic
track: Research track. The tool collects, analyses, and synthesises multi-modal session data and outputs structured research findings.
platform: Cursor + Python with a Streamlit interface.
rationale: This project requires real computation across multiple modalities and cannot be built in Lovable or Bolt. The output report is generative rather than templated: its structure is determined by what the analysis actually found, so a session dominated by navigation friction produces a different report than one with evenly distributed issues. A conversational query layer lets the researcher ask for specific findings in natural language after the report is generated, which means the interface itself is produced in response to the conversation rather than being a fixed dashboard. Both of these directly reflect the generative UI concept where the output format reflects the content rather than following a pre-built template.
title: Multi-Modal Usability Session Analyzer

problem: A tool for freelance UX/UI consultants that automatically audits client websites for accessibility issues, design inconsistencies, and information architecture problems, so they do not have to manually inspect and document every issue across each new project.
audience: The primary users are freelance UX/UI designers, UX consultants, and UX engineers who frequently onboard new client websites. Clients and product teams benefit from faster audits, clearer UX findings, and more consistent improvement recommendations.
data: The tool collects publicly available website data including HTML structure, CSS styles, typography, colors, navigation hierarchy, accessibility attributes, and performance metrics, then produces structured audit reports, visual summaries, and categorized UX findings.
track: Design track
rationale: Claude Code will be used as the development environment to write and organize the project code, while GitHub Pages will be used to deploy and host the final web application. This setup supports building a lightweight browser-based UX audit tool that can be easily shared, tested, and accessed online.
title: Automated Website UX Audit Tool

problem: UX designers and design teams struggle to ideate quickly and stay organized. Brainstorming on paper, stickies, or documents is easy but produces scattered, hard-to-use outputs, and there is no guided digital tool that pushes people to think boldly at volume while keeping ideas structured for next steps.
audience: UX designers and design students, working solo or in small teams of 2–8 people. They benefit by leaving ideation sessions with organized, actionable concept directions rather than a pile of unprocessed sticky notes.
data: The tool accepts two types of text input, pain points or research findings (which the AI converts into HMW questions), or a HMW question typed directly by the user, and produces time-boxed brainstorm prompts for a Crazy 8s session via the Anthropic API.
track: Design track.
rationale: This project requires conditional logic, timed interactions, and phase transitions (from HMW generation into a Crazy 8s session) that need real interactive behavior beyond a static UI. Bolt handles that complexity while keeping the build low-code, which matches the two-week timeline and a focus on interaction design over engineering.
title: AI-Guided Crazy 8s Brainstorm Facilitator

problem: A tool that takes raw usability session notes and produces a privacy audit, flagging PII passages, explaining the regulatory risk of each, and outputting a redacted version, so UX researchers can safely feed session data into AI analysis tools without exposing participant information or violating informed consent.
audience: UX researchers and research operations teams who use AI tools to analyze session data but have no structured way to screen for participant privacy risks before doing so. They benefit by being able to move faster on AI-assisted synthesis without compromising participant trust or GDPR compliance.
data: The tool takes raw text input (pasted session notes or transcripts) from the researcher and produces two outputs: a structured privacy audit flagging sensitive passages with risk explanations, and a cleaned text file with PII removed or anonymized.
track: Research track. The tool processes and transforms data; outputs are structured findings (the audit) and a research-ready artifact (the redacted notes).
rationale: The core work is computation: detecting sensitive text patterns, classifying risk, and transforming the input into a safe output, which is exactly what Python is built for. There is no UI that needs to be the product; the value is entirely in what the tool produces.
title: Session Notes Privacy Audit Tool

problem: Children ages 6–12 often get either passive digital “page-flip” books or overstimulating games that pull them away from the story, so they miss chances to choose, explore, and feel progress inside a narrative; this project is an interactive storybook that weaves branching choices, tap-to-discover moments, light puzzles, visible progress, and read-aloud into one gentle adventure so reading stays playful and intentional instead of mindless tapping or pure spectacle.
audience: Primary users are children ages 6–12 reading on a phone, tablet, or laptop in a browser. Parents, caregivers, and elementary educators benefit when kids can read solo or together with clear navigation, rewarding progress, and a calm, story-first experience that supports attention and enjoyment without needing the adult to manage the app constantly.
data: The app uses and produces structured story data (scene text, illustration references, branching choices, hotspot configs, and mini-game rules) as JSON/JS in the repo, plus image and audio assets and locally stored reading progress (e.g., stars and current scene)—authored and versioned in the project, with no external research dataset required.
track: Design track
platform: Cursor (? currently use Cursor, but maybe combine using Cursor and other AI tools - Lovable or Bolt)
rationale: The product is experienced primarily through its interface—the story, art, touch interactions, and audio are the deliverable—not a data-analysis pipeline. Cursor fits because the work is building and iterating that UI in HTML/CSS/JavaScript with branching logic and games, while keeping everything in the HCDE git repo (including .cursorrules and notes) for MP2 submission, portfolio review, and GitHub Pages deployment; Python-heavy computation is not the core of this project.
title: Interactive Branching Storybook for Children

problem: Amateur and recreational football players in the US and China play almost exclusively on artificial grass (AG) or turf (TF) pitches, yet the market is saturated with FG (firm ground) boots and product information is fragmented across brand sites, review blogs, and forums — leaving players to manually cross-reference 20+ sources to figure out which boot actually fits their pitch, position, and budget.
audience: Amateur and semi-amateur football players aged 18–35 who play 1–3 times a week on AG/TF surfaces and care about gear but lack the time (or domain language) to navigate professional-tier marketing. Coaches and recreational team captains who get asked "what should I buy?" by teammates also benefit.
data: The tool draws on a curated dataset of ~150 current and recent football boots (compiled from footballbootsdb.com archives and brand product pages) with fields for model, brand, surface type (FG/AG/SG/TF/HG/IC), price tier, weight, upper material, and player-position fit; the output is a ranked shortlist with side-by-side comparisons.
track:
Design track
 — the tool is experienced through its interface. The whole point is that a player can answer 3–4 questions ("what surface? what position? what budget?") and walk away with a clear recommendation. The UI 
is
 the product.
rationale: This project lives or dies on the interface: an amateur player won't read a CSV or a notebook, they want a clean comparison view they can use on their phone before going to the store. The computation involved is simple filtering and ranking — no heavy data processing — so Lovable's strength in shipping a polished, deployable UI fast is the right match, rather than Cursor's strength in computation-heavy notebooks.
title: Football Boot Surface Match Recommender

problem: A desktop coding companion (look will be Claude's mascot) that gives vibe coders lightweight emotional feedback and progress cues while they work with Claude Code, so they do not have to rely only on terminal text, logs, or static IDE status indicators to understand what the agent is doing.
audience: The primary users are student designers, creative technologists, and beginner developers who use Claude Code or similar coding agents while building projects. The people who benefit are learners who want coding to feel less intimidating, more playful, and more legible during long agent-assisted work sessions.
data: It uses Claude Code session states, terminal events, user-triggered actions, and optional project status signals, then turns them into animated behavioral states such as thinking, coding, stuck, celebrating, waiting, or error-recovering.
track: Design track. The value is experienced mainly through the interface and interaction: the animated crab companion, its behaviors, and how it makes coding feel more approachable.
rationale: This project needs more than a static interface because the Claude mascot should react to changing coding states, user actions, and conditional events like errors, waiting, success, or idle time. I think Bolt is the best fit because the core challenge is designing interactive behavior with logic.
title: Animated Claude Coding Companion

problem: UX researchers, product designers, PMs, and research students need to turn large volumes of qualitative inputs (quotes, notes, feedback) into themes, and currently they must manually read, code, and affinity-cluster data for hours before they can synthesize findings.
audience:
A
udience: Primary users are UX researchers, product designers, PMs, and students conducting user research who need fast but credible thematic analysis. Secondary beneficiaries are cross-functional teammates and stakeholders who rely on clearer, shareable, and privacy-safe insight outputs for decisions.
data: The tool ingests pasted text or uploaded CSV/TXT/DOC/DOCX qualitative data, auto-anonymizes personal identifiers, and produces structured multi-level themes, cluster assignments with one-sentence rationales, participant-linked visual encodings, and exportable artifacts (CSV/PDF/FigJam).
track: Research track.
rationale: This project requires real computation-heavy workflows (file parsing, PII masking, LLM-driven clustering, hierarchy generation, role-aware data handling), which fits Cursor best. The interface matters, but the core value is robust analysis and transformation of qualitative data rather than lightweight UI assembly alone.
title: Qualitative Data Auto-Clustering Tool
